arXiv:1209.3194v2 [math.AP] 20 Sep 2013

The Linearized 2D Inviscid Shallow Water Equations in a Rectangle: Boundary conditions and well-posedness

Aimin Huang and Roger Temam Address: The Institute for Scientific Computing and Applied Mathematics, Indiana University, 831 East Third Street, Rawles Hall, Bloomington, Indiana 47405, U.S.A. Email address: AH:aimhuang@indiana.edu Email address: RT:temam@indiana.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We consider the linearized 2D inviscid shallow water equations in a rectangle. A set of boundary conditions is proposed which make these equations well-posed. Several different cases occur depending on the relative values of the reference velocities (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) and reference height ϕ0\phi_{0} (sub- or super-critical flow at each part of the boundary).

1. Introduction

Motivated by the study of the inviscid linearized primitive equation (as a step towards the study of the full nonlinear equations), we consider in this article the linearized fully inviscid shallow water equations in a rectangle. To the best of our knowledge, the well-posedness of the linearized inviscid shallow water equations in a rectangle has not yet been addressed. In particular, the existence of corners in the geometrical domain is a subject of mathematical concern since the seminal works [Osh73, Osh74] which show the possible occurrence of major singularities in the corners for certain choices of the boundary conditions. The boundary conditions that we choose do not lead to singularities and allow us to develop results of existence and uniqueness of solution in suitable spaces to be described later on.

In this article, the well-posedness of the linearized inviscid shallow water equations is classically conducted using the linear semigroup theory. We write these equations as an abstract evolution equation in a Hilbert space:

d​Ud​t+A​U=F,\frac{\text{d}U}{\text{d}t}+AU=F,

with initial data U⁡(0)=U0U(0)=U_{0} given, which means that we prescribe the boundary conditions at t=0t=0 (see below). In this approach, the main difficulty is to show that ⟨A​U,U⟩≥0\langle AU,U\rangle\geq 0 for all UU in the domain 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) of AA (and similarly ⟨A∗​U,U⟩≥0,∀U∈𝒟⁡(A∗)\langle A^{*}U,U\rangle\geq 0,\,\forall U\in\mathcal{D}(A^{*})), where AA is the abstract associated operator acting in L2​(Ω)3L^{2}(\Omega)^{3} and A∗A^{*} is its adjoint. This result is achieved using a suitable approximation technique. Two main different cases occur depending on whether the linearized base flow with velocities (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) and height ϕ0\phi_{0} is fully hyperbolic or partially hyperbolic and partially elliptic. The fully hyperbolic case corresponding to u02+v02>g​ϕ0u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0} contains four sub-cases depending on whether the flow is sub- or super-critical on each side of the rectangle (u02,v02>u_{0}^{2},v_{0}^{2}> or <g​ϕ0<g\phi_{0}). The elliptic-hyperbolic case corresponding to u02+v02<g​ϕ0u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0} is fully subcritical (u02,v02<g​ϕ0)(u_{0}^{2},v_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0}); furthermore the time independent part of the shallow water equations is partly elliptic in this case, but of course the full shallow water system remains hyperbolic. Boundary value problems of the Dirichlet or Neumann type appear in this case. Of course the presence of the corners also raises difficulties for these elliptic problems, but the desired regularity of the solutions of the corresponding Dirichlet-Neumann problem is achieved using results from [Gri85] which produce restrictions on the domain if other domains than rectangles were to be considered (see Remark 5.1 at the end).

The study of the Local Area Models (LAMs) in the atmosphere and oceans sciences, leads to initial and boundary value problems for the inviscid primitive equations in these domains, and we know since [OS78] (see also [TT03]) that these problems are complicated leading to nonlocal boundary value problems. As explained in e.g. [WPT97] the choice of the boundary condition is important for the numerical simulations, as one wishes boundary conditions leading to well-posed problems (to avoid numerical explosion) and boundary conditions that are transparent, letting the waves move freely inside and outside the domain. In the perspective of a LAM imbedded in a large domain, any such set of conditions is acceptable.

The linearized shallow water equations (SWE) that we consider read

(1.1) {ut+u0​ux+v0​uy+g​ϕx−f​v=0,vt+u0​vx+v0​vy+g​ϕy+f​u=0,ϕt+u0​ϕx+v0​ϕy+ϕ0​(ux+vy)=0;\begin{cases}u_{t}+u_{0}u_{x}+v_{0}u_{y}+g\phi_{x}-fv=0,\\ v_{t}+u_{0}v_{x}+v_{0}v_{y}+g\phi_{y}+fu=0,\\ \phi_{t}+u_{0}\phi_{x}+v_{0}\phi_{y}+\phi_{0}(u_{x}+v_{y})=0;\end{cases}

here U=(u,v,ϕ)t,(x,y)∈Ω:=(0,L1)×(0,L2)U=(u,v,\phi)^{t},(x,y)\in\Omega:=(0,L_{1})\times(0,L_{2}), u0,v0,ϕ0u_{0},v_{0},\phi_{0} are positive constants, and gg is the gravitational acceleration, ff is the Coriolis parameter. As explained in e.g. [OS78, TT03, RTT08b], the inviscid primitive equations in a cube can be expanded in vertical modes expansion producing a set of coupled bi-dimensional equations, similar to coupled shallow water equations. For one linearized mode, the system that we obtain is very similar to (1.1) as we show at the end of this article. With this respect the results that we obtain for the one-mode linearized primitive equations generalize in part the results from [RTT08b] in which we assumed v0=0v_{0}=0; the full coupled system as considered in [RTT08b] will be studied elsewhere.

As we know the literature on the shallow water equations is very vast, both on the theoretical and computational aspects, considering the viscous equations or the partly or totally inviscid equations and considering that the height is either always strictly positive or that it can vanish. See e.g. [AB03, ABBKP, ABPS, BC01, BP91, BPSTT, SLTT] on the computational side and see e.g. [BD03, BDM07, BN07, Bre09, BR11, HPT11, PT11, KU82, KU88, KU89, Ore95, Ush83] on the theoretical side. But as we said we did not find this problem studied in the literature. The general hyperbolic equations in a domain with corners are also considered in [Tan78, KT80], but the boundary conditions they imposed is different from ours, and the space they used is not the usual L2L^{2} space which we use in this article. Closest to our article is the book [BS07] which systematically studies the initial and boundary value problems for linear hyperbolic equations but the spatial domain is smooth. Close to our article also are the articles [Osh73, Osh74] which study the boundary value problem for hyperbolic equations in domains with corners; various singularities can occur near the corners of the domain. More precisely in [Osh74], the two dimensional shallow water equations are linearized around a constant flow as we do, and the boundary conditions are Dirichlet boundary conditions for linear combinations of the components as ours. Theorem 2.6 of [Osh74] provides situations (a~)(\tilde{a}) which produces a lack of uniqueness and (b~)(\tilde{b}) which produces a lack of existence of solution. None of the examples provided in [Osh74] is consistent with the boundary conditions that we propose. Note that [Osh74] deals with a quarter plane x>0,y>0x>0,y>0, but we believe that the situation is (or should be) the same as ours at the corners. Note also that our initial motivation related to LAMs is already expressed in [Osh74] though in a more succinct way (middle of page 155). Also as suggested in [Osh74], for any reasonable theory for hyperbolic boundary value problem, the solution will enjoy the finite speed propagation property so that at least in what we call below ”the fully hyperbolic case”, we could instead of a rectangle, have considered a single wedge or a more general polygonal domain. However this is not the case in what we call below the ”elliptic-hyperbolic case”. Also we preferred to work in a rectangular domain to stay close from the initial motivation in ocean and atmosphere science.

Beyond our initial motivation related to the primitive equations and the LAMs in climate and weather studies, this work can be seen as a first step in studying the initial and boundary value problems for hyperbolic equations in non-smooth domains. Although the subject is very vast, we intend to extend this work in a few directions. Firstly, for linear equations, we intend to consider more general hyperbolic systems and possibly other convex polygons (pentagon, hexagon, etc). Secondly, we intend to study the nonlinear inviscid shallow water equations; see already the two cases considered in [HPT12, HT12b]. Note that to study the nonlinear SWE we will probably need to study the equations linearized around a time dependent flow. This is not the case in this article but this occurs in [HPT12, HT12b].

A marking point of this study is that, in certain cases, the (time independent part of the) fully hyperbolic system contains a system which is partly hyperbolic and partly elliptic; this fact is probably general and appears also in classical compressible fluid mechanics where the stationary flow can be subsonic, sonic or supersonic that is governed by elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic equations (see e.g. [CF48]). For this reason, this article stands at the interface between hyperbolic equations and parabolic-elliptic equations, but the methods used are rather those of parabolic and elliptic equations; this includes a regularization technique of L. Hörmander [Hor65] and regularity results by P. Grisvard [Gri85] for solutions of elliptic equations in polygonal domains.

This article is organized as follows. At the end of this introductory section, we study the associated stationary system and find that the stationary system can be decoupled into some simple equations. Then in the technical Section 2, we present a useful trace theorem and derive various density theorems, density of certain smooth functions in certain function spaces. It prepares to the necessary density results needed in Section 3 in which we study the stationary shallow water equations operator in the fully hyperbolic case when u02+v02>g​ϕ0u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0}. Section 4 is devoted to the study of the stationary shallow water equations operator in the elliptic-hyperbolic case when u02+v02<g​ϕ0u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0}, where we first prove a regularity result for an associated elliptic problem. In Section 5 we state the general existence and uniqueness theorem proved by application of the Hille-Phillips-Yoshida theorem, which covers all cases (all respective values of u0,v0,ϕ0u_{0},v_{0},\phi_{0} indicated above). We also make the connection with the equations for one mode of the linearized primitive equations and interpret our earlier result for that case and briefly show that the results can be extended to the case of non-homogeneous boundary conditions.

2. Trace and density theorems

2.1. A trace theorem

Since we have to assign boundary conditions on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, we first need to make sure that the desired traces at the boundary make sense for the functional setting that we will use. Thus we consider the space:

𝒳(Ω)={U∈H=L2(Ω)3,𝒜U∈H},\mathcal{X}(\Omega)=\{U\in H=L^{2}(\Omega)^{3},\mathcal{A}U\in H\},

endowed with its natural Hilbert norm (‖U‖H2+‖𝒜​U‖H2)1/2(\left\|U\right\|_{H}^{2}+\left\|\mathcal{A}U\right\|_{H}^{2})^{1/2}. Then we have the following trace result.

Proposition 2.1.

2.2. The density theorems

In this subsection, we establish general density theorems regarding functions defined on the domain Ω=(0,L1)×(0,L2)\Omega=(0,L_{1})\times(0,L_{2}). These theorems will be needed for proving later on that −A-A is the infinitesimal generator of a semigroup of contraction, where AA is the abstract operator associated with 𝒜\mathcal{A} and with certain boundary conditions to be chosen in each case separately.

For λ\lambda fixed, λ∈ℝ,λ≠0\lambda\in\mathbb{R},\lambda\neq 0, we set T​θ=θy+λ​θxT\theta=\theta_{y}+\lambda\theta_{x}, and introduce the function space

𝒳1(Ω)={θ∈L2(Ω),Tθ=θy+λθx∈L2(Ω)}.\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega)=\{\theta\in L^{2}(\Omega),T\theta=\theta_{y}+\lambda\theta_{x}\in L^{2}(\Omega)\}.

We need to show that the smooth functions are dense in 𝒳1​(Ω)\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega). Later on we will prove more involved density theorems, showing that if u∈𝒳1​(Ω)u\in\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega) vanishes on certain parts of ∂Ω\partial\Omega, then uu can be approximated in 𝒳1​(Ω)\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega) by smooth functions, vanishing on the same parts of the boundary. We first have the following.

Proposition 2.2.

𝒞∞​(Ω¯)∩𝒳1​(Ω)\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega})\cap\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega) is dense in 𝒳1​(Ω)\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega).

The proof of Proposition 2.2 is classically conducted by using the method of partition of unity, hence we omit it here.

Remark 2.1.

Proposition 2.2 is also valid with TT replaced by any first order differential operator with constant coefficients.

We are now going to prove the density theorems involving the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, and we will successively consider the scalar case and the vector case. Since we have to assign boundary conditions on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, we first need to make sure that the desired traces at the boundary make sense. We actually have the following result proven exactly as in Proposition 2.1.

Proposition 2.3.

If θ∈𝒳1​(Ω)\theta\in\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega), then the traces of θ\theta are defined on all of ∂Ω\partial\Omega, i.e. the traces of uu are defined at x=0,L1x=0,L_{1}, and y=0,L2y=0,L_{2}, and they belong to the respective spaces Hy−1​(0,L2)H_{y}^{-1}(0,L_{2}) and Hx−1​(0,L1)H_{x}^{-1}(0,L_{1}). Furthermore the trace operators are linear continuous in the corresponding spaces, e.g., θ∈𝒳1​(Ω)→θ|x=0\theta\in\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega)\rightarrow\theta|_{x=0} is continuous from 𝒳1​(Ω)\mathcal{X}_{1}(\Omega) into Hy−1​(0,L2)H_{y}^{-1}(0,L_{2}).

For any function vv defined on Ω\Omega, here and again in the following we denote by v~\tilde{v} the function equal to vv in Ω\Omega and to 00 in ℝ2\Ω\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\Omega. In the scalar case, we introduce the function spaces:

(2.4) 𝒳Γ(Ω)={θ∈L2(Ω),Tθ=θy+λθx∈L2(Ω),θ|Γ=0},\mathcal{X}_{\Gamma}(\Omega)=\{\theta\in L^{2}(\Omega),T\theta=\theta_{y}+\lambda\theta_{x}\in L^{2}(\Omega),\theta|_{\Gamma}=0\},

Theorem 2.1.

Looking carefully at the proof of Theorem 2.1, we see that Theorem 2.1 is also valid when Γ\Gamma is made of two contiguous sides of ∂Ω\partial\Omega, that is in the following three cases:

Theorem 2.2.

and introduce the function spaces in the vector case:

Then we have

3. The fully hyperbolic case

In this section, we study the stationary 2D shallow water equations operator for the fully hyperbolic case where Δ=u02+v02−g​ϕ0\Delta=u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0} is positive. We have four sub-cases to consider depending on the signs of u02−g​ϕ0u_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0} and v02−g​ϕ0v_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0}, and we call them the supercritical case, the mixed hyperbolic case (two sub-cases) and the fully hyperbolic subcritical case; we will study these cases in the following subsections. We should bear in mind the fully decoupled system (1.3) in this case, and it is easy to see that

a1,a3,b2,b3>0,a_{1},\,a_{3},\,b_{2},\,b_{3}>0,

since u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} and ϕ0\phi_{0} are all positive, and the signs of a2a_{2} and b1b_{1} depend on the signs of u02−g​ϕ0u_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0} and v02−g​ϕ0v_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0} respectively.

3.1. The supercritical case

The supercritical (fully supersonic) case corresponds to the case where:

(3.1) u02>g​ϕ0,v02>g​ϕ0.u_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0},\hskip 6.0ptv_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0}.

Under assumption (3.1), we see that a2a_{2} and b1b_{1} are both positive and we conclude that

ai,bi>0,∀i=1,2,3.a_{i},\,b_{i}>0,\quad\quad\forall\,i=1,2,3.

According to the general hyperbolic theory, we choose the boundary conditions for the incoming characteristics, hence, we choose the boundary conditions for (ξ,η,ζ)(\xi,\eta,\zeta) at x=0x=0 and y=0y=0 since aia_{i} and bib_{i} (i=1,2,3i=1,2,3) are all positive, which is equivalent to choose the boundary conditions for U=(u,v,ϕ)U=(u,v,\phi) at x=0x=0 and y=0y=0, i.e.

(3.2) {u=v=ϕ=0, on ΓW={x=0},u=v=ϕ=0, on ΓS={y=0}.\begin{cases}u=v=\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}=\{x=0\},\\ u=v=\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{S}=\{y=0\}.\end{cases}

We then define the unbounded operator AA on H=L2​(Ω)3H=L^{2}(\Omega)^{3}, with A​U=𝒜​U,∀U∈𝒟⁡(A)AU=\mathcal{A}U,\,\forall U\in\mathcal{D}(A) and

(3.3) U​ vanishes in a neighborhood of ​ΓW∪ΓS,U\text{ vanishes in a neighborhood of }\Gamma_{W}\cup\Gamma_{S},

and the function space:

Setting Γ→=(ΓW∪ΓS,ΓW∪ΓS,ΓW∪ΓS)\vec{\Gamma}=(\Gamma_{W}\cup\Gamma_{S},\Gamma_{W}\cup\Gamma_{S},\Gamma_{W}\cup\Gamma_{S}), we have that P^−1​U|Γ→=0\hat{P}^{-1}U|_{\vec{\Gamma}}=0 is equivalent to (3.2) and P^−1​U\hat{P}^{-1}U vanishing in a neighborhood of Γ→\vec{\Gamma} is the same as (3.3), where P^\hat{P} is as in (1.6). Then we obtain the following result from Theorem 2.2 with Q=P^−1,M1=ℰ1,M2=ℰ2,Λ=diag​(λ1,λ2,λ3)Q=\hat{P}^{-1},M_{1}=\mathcal{E}_{1},M_{2}=\mathcal{E}_{2},\Lambda=\text{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}).

Lemma 3.1.

𝒱⁡(Ω)∩𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{V}(\Omega)\cap\mathcal{D}(A) is dense in 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A).

3.1.1. Positivity of AA and its adjoint A∗A^{*}

We endow the space H=L2​(Ω)3H=L^{2}(\Omega)^{3} with the Hilbert scalar product and norm:

⟨U,U¯⟩H=∫Ω(u​u¯+v​v¯+gϕ0​ϕ​ϕ¯)​d​x​d​y=∫ΩU¯t​S0​U​d​x​d​y,‖U‖H={⟨U,U⟩H}1/2.\langle U,\overline{U}\rangle_{H}=\int_{\Omega}(u\bar{u}+v\bar{v}+\frac{g}{\phi_{0}}\phi\bar{\phi})\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int_{\Omega}\overline{U}^{t}S_{0}U\,\text{d}x\text{d}y},\hskip 6.0pt\left\|U\right\|_{H}=\{\langle U,U\rangle_{H}\}^{1/2}.

Our aim is to prove that AA and its adjoint A∗A^{*} defined below are positive in the sense,

(3.4) {⟨AU,U⟩H≥0,∀U∈𝒟(A),⟨A∗U,U⟩H≥0,∀U∈𝒟(A∗).\begin{cases}\langle AU,U\rangle_{H}\geq 0,\hskip 6.0pt\forall U\in\mathcal{D}(A),\\ \langle A^{*}U,U\rangle_{H}\geq 0,\hskip 6.0pt\forall U\in\mathcal{D}(A^{*}).\end{cases}

These properties are needed to apply the Hille-Phillips-Yoshida theorem (see [Yos80, HP74]), see below. The result for AA is now easy thanks to Lemma 3.1. Indeed the following calculations are easy, for UU smooth in 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A):

(3.5) ⟨A​U,U⟩H=∫Ω(u0​ux+v0​uy+g​ϕx)​u+(u0​vx+v0​vy+g​ϕy)​v+gϕ0​(u0​ϕx+v0​ϕy+ϕ0​(ux+vy))​ϕ​d​x​d​y=(using integration by parts)=∫0L2(u02​(u2+v2+gϕ0​ϕ2)+g​ϕ​u)|x=0x=L1​d​y+∫0L1(v02(u2+v2+gϕ0ϕ2)+gϕv)|y=0y=L2dx=I1+I2+I3+I4,\begin{split}\langle AU,U\rangle_{H}&=\int_{\Omega}(u_{0}u_{x}+v_{0}u_{y}+g\phi_{x})u+(u_{0}v_{x}+v_{0}v_{y}+g\phi_{y})v\\ &\hskip 20.0pt+\frac{g}{\phi_{0}}(u_{0}\phi_{x}+v_{0}\phi_{y}+\phi_{0}(u_{x}+v_{y}))\phi\,\text{d}x\text{d}y\\ &=(\text{using integration by parts})\\ &=\int_{0}^{L_{2}}\big(\frac{u_{0}}{2}(u^{2}+v^{2}+\frac{g}{\phi_{0}}\phi^{2})+g\phi u\big)\Big|_{x=0}^{x=L_{1}}\text{d}y\\ &\hskip 20.0pt+\int_{0}^{L_{1}}\big(\frac{v_{0}}{2}(u^{2}+v^{2}+\frac{g}{\phi_{0}}\phi^{2})+g\phi v\big)\Big|_{y=0}^{y=L_{2}}\text{d}x\\ &=I_{1}+I_{2}+I_{3}+I_{4},\end{split}

where I1,I2,I3,I4I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4} respectively stand for the boundary terms at x=0x=0, x=L1x=L_{1}, y=0y=0 and y=L2y=L_{2}. First, the boundary conditions (3.2) imply that I1=I3=0I_{1}=I_{3}=0. We then rewrite I2,I4I_{2},I_{4} as:

I2=u02​[(u+gu0​ϕ)2+g2​(1g​ϕ0−1u02)​ϕ2+v2]​(L1,y),I4=v02​[(v+gv0​ϕ)2+g2​(1g​ϕ0−1v02)​ϕ2+u2]​(x,L2),\begin{split}I_{2}=\frac{u_{0}}{2}\big[(u+\frac{g}{u_{0}}\phi)^{2}+g^{2}(\frac{1}{g\phi_{0}}-\frac{1}{u_{0}^{2}})\phi^{2}+v^{2}\big](L_{1},y),\\ I_{4}=\frac{v_{0}}{2}\big[(v+\frac{g}{v_{0}}\phi)^{2}+g^{2}(\frac{1}{g\phi_{0}}-\frac{1}{v_{0}^{2}})\phi^{2}+u^{2}\big](x,L_{2}),\end{split}

which are nonnegative under assumption (3.1). Therefore, we conclude that ⟨A​U,U⟩H≥0\langle AU,U\rangle_{H}\geq 0 for UU smooth in 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A), which is also valid for all UU in 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) thanks to Lemma 3.1.

We now turn to the definition of the formal adjoint A∗A^{*} of AA and its domain 𝒟⁡(A∗)\mathcal{D}(A^{*}), in the sense of the adjoint of a linear unbounded operator (see [Rud91]). For that purpose we first assume that U∈𝒟⁡(A)U\in\mathcal{D}(A) and U¯∈H\overline{U}\in H are smooth functions, and then compute

(3.6) ⟨A​U,U¯⟩H=∫Ω(u0​ux+v0​uy+g​ϕx)​u¯+(u0​vx+v0​vy+g​ϕy)​v¯+gϕ0​(u0​ϕx+v0​ϕy+ϕ0​(ux+vy))​ϕ¯​d​x​d​y=J0+J1,\begin{split}\langle AU,\overline{U}\rangle_{H}&=\int_{\Omega}(u_{0}u_{x}+v_{0}u_{y}+g\phi_{x})\bar{u}+(u_{0}v_{x}+v_{0}v_{y}+g\phi_{y})\bar{v}\\ &\hskip 20.0pt+\frac{g}{\phi_{0}}\big(u_{0}\phi_{x}+v_{0}\phi_{y}+\phi_{0}(u_{x}+v_{y})\big)\bar{\phi}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y\\ &=J_{0}+J_{1},\end{split}

where J0J_{0} stands for the integral on Ω\Omega and J1J_{1} for the integral on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. For J0J_{0}, we have:

4. The elliptic-hyperbolic case

We aim in this section to study the elliptic-hyperbolic case (we also call it the mixed subcritical case) which corresponds to

(4.1) u02+v02<g​ϕ0,implying​u02<g​ϕ0,v02<g​ϕ0,u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 5.0pt\text{implying}\hskip 5.0ptu_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 3.0ptv_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},

and which embodies some elliptic operators.

4.1. A preliminary regularity theorem

In this subsection, we introduce some necessary preliminary results for the elliptic operator embodied in the stationary 2D shallow water equations operator, namely we prove some theorems regarding functions defined on the domain Ω=(0,L1)×(0,L2)\Omega=(0,L_{1})\times(0,L_{2}). These theorems will be very useful in verifying the positivity of the elliptic mode in the shallow water equations operator in Subsection 4.2. Using the notations in Subsection 2.2, we introduce the following boundary conditions:

In conclusion, in the new coordinate system (x′,y′)(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}), we find a unique solution Θ′\Theta^{\prime} that belongs to V′V^{\prime}, and solves the problem 𝒯​Θ′=Ψ′\mathcal{T}\Theta^{\prime}=\Psi^{\prime}. The uniqueness in 𝒟⁡(𝒯)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{T}) amounts now to showing that 𝒯\mathcal{T} is one to one on 𝒟⁡(𝒯)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{T}), that is 𝒯​Θ=0\mathcal{T}\Theta=0 implies Θ=0\Theta=0. Theorem 4.2.

We assume that (4.3) holds. Then the operator 𝒯\mathcal{T} is positive, i.e. ⟨𝒯​Θ,Θ⟩≥0\langle\mathcal{T}\Theta,\Theta\rangle\geq 0 holds for any Θ∈𝒟⁡(𝒯)=V\Theta\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{T})=V.

⟨𝒯​Θ,Θ⟩=∫ΩΘt​T1​Θx+Θt​T2​Θy​d​x​d​y=12​∫0L2Θt​T1​Θ|x=0x=L1​d​y+12​∫0L1Θt​T2​Θ|y=0y=L2​d​x≥0,\begin{split}\langle\mathcal{T}\Theta,\Theta\rangle&=\int_{\Omega}\Theta^{t}T_{1}\Theta_{x}+\Theta^{t}T_{2}\Theta_{y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{L_{2}}\Theta^{t}T_{1}\Theta\Big|_{x=0}^{x=L_{1}}\text{d}y+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{L_{1}}\Theta^{t}T_{2}\Theta\Big|_{y=0}^{y=L_{2}}\text{d}x\\ &\geq 0,\end{split}

where we used the boundary conditions (4.2) and the assumption α1,α2>0\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}>0. ∎

Theorem 4.3.

Let l⁡(Θ¯)=⟨F,𝒯​Θ¯⟩l(\overline{\Theta})=\langle F,\mathcal{T}\overline{\Theta}\rangle and a⁡(Θ,Θ¯)=⟨𝒯​Θ,𝒯​Θ¯⟩L2​(Ω)2a(\Theta,\overline{\Theta})=\langle\mathcal{T}\Theta,\mathcal{T}\overline{\Theta}\rangle_{L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}}; then it is not hard to check that the linear form ll is continuous on VV, and the bilinear form aa is continuous on V×VV\times V. (4.22) a⁡(Θ,Θ¯)=l⁡(Θ¯),a(\Theta,\overline{\Theta})=l(\overline{\Theta}),

for all Θ¯∈V\overline{\Theta}\in V thanks to the Lax-Milgram Theorem.

We now interpret (4.22) in the distribution sense. For any Ψ∈𝒟​(Ω)2\Psi\in\mathcal{D}(\Omega)^{2}, we find Θ¯∈V\overline{\Theta}\in V such that 𝒯​Θ¯=Ψ\mathcal{T}\overline{\Theta}=\Psi by virtue of Proposition 4.1, and then (4.22) shows that 𝒯​Θ=F\mathcal{T}\Theta=F in the sense of distributions, and hence in L2​(Ω)2L^{2}(\Omega)^{2} since 𝒟​(Ω)2\mathcal{D}(\Omega)^{2} is dense in L2​(Ω)2L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}. ∎

Theorem 4.5.

The space 𝒟~​(𝒯∗)\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) is the space V¯\overline{V}.

Finally we define the function space

V¯♯={Ξ=(ξ1,ξ2)t∈H1​(Ω′)2|Ξ​ satisfies ( ♯  ‣ 4.1.2) }.\overline{V}^{\sharp}=\{\Xi=(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})^{t}\in H^{1}(\Omega^{\prime})^{2}\ |\ \Xi\text{ satisfies \eqref{eq:eq6.29} }\}.

We are now seeking Ξ∈V¯♯\Xi\in\overline{V}^{\sharp} satisfying 𝒫​Ξ=Ψ\mathcal{P}\Xi=\Psi, that is

(4.34) {−ξ1​x′−ξ2​y′=ψ1,ξ1​y′−ξ2​x′=ψ2.\begin{cases}-\xi_{1x^{\prime}}-\xi_{2y^{\prime}}=\psi_{1},\\ \xi_{1y^{\prime}}-\xi_{2x^{\prime}}=\psi_{2}.\end{cases}

We now have two cases to consider. First, if μ1=0\mu_{1}=0, then the boundary conditions ( ♯ ‣ 4.1.2) are simpler, and similar to the boundary conditions ( ′ ‣ 4.1.1). Hence, we obtain a unique solution Ξ∈V¯♭\Xi\in\overline{V}^{\flat} that solves the problem 𝒫​Ξ=Ψ\mathcal{P}\Xi=\Psi by following the same arguments as for Proposition 4.1. If μ1≠0\mu_{1}\neq 0, then without loss of generality, we can assume that μ1=1\mu_{1}=1, and the arguments presented below will be similar to the proof of Proposition 4.1.

Differentiating (4.34)1\eqref{eq:eq6.30}_{1} with respect to y′y^{\prime} and (4.34)2\eqref{eq:eq6.30}_{2} with respect to x′x^{\prime}, and summing these two equations, we find

(4.35) Δ′​ξ2=−ψ1​y′−ψ2​x′.\Delta^{\prime}\xi_{2}=-\psi_{1y^{\prime}}-\psi_{2x^{\prime}}.

We first associate with equation (4.35) the boundary condition

(4.36) ξ2=0, on ​ΓW′,\xi_{2}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}^{\prime},

which is already contained in ( ♯ ‣ 4.1.2). For the other boundaries, suitable boundary conditions can be obtained as follows. As in Proposition 4.1, we denote by νi′\nu_{i}^{\prime} the unit normal vector to Γi′\Gamma_{i}^{\prime}, and τi′\tau_{i}^{\prime} the unit tangent vector on Γi′\Gamma_{i}^{\prime}, for all i∈{W,E,S,N}i\in\{W,E,S,N\}. On ΓE′\Gamma_{E}^{\prime}, we have ∂ξ1/∂τ2′=0\partial\xi_{1}/\partial\tau_{2}^{\prime}=0 since ξ1=0\xi_{1}=0 on ΓE′\Gamma_{E}^{\prime}. Noticing that (0,1)(0,1) is parallel to τ2′\tau_{2}^{\prime}, we find that ξ1​y′=0\xi_{1y^{\prime}}=0, which, together with (4.34)2\eqref{eq:eq6.30}_{2}, implies that ξ2​x′=−ξ1​y′=0\xi_{2x^{\prime}}=-\xi_{1y^{\prime}}=0 by noticing that ψ2\psi_{2} vanishes on ΓE′\Gamma_{E}^{\prime}. Observing that νE′\nu_{E}^{\prime} is parallel to (1,0)(1,0), we then associate to (4.35) the following boundary condition on ΓE′\Gamma_{E}^{\prime}:

(4.37) ∂ξ2∂νE′=0, on ​ΓE′.\frac{\partial\xi_{2}}{\partial\nu_{E}^{\prime}}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{E}^{\prime}.

Similar arguments show that we need to associate to (4.35) the following condition on the other two boundaries:

(4.38) {∂ξ2∂νS′−∂ξ2∂τS′=0, on ​ΓS′,∂ξ2∂νN′+∂ξ2∂τN′=0, on ​ΓN′.\begin{cases}\frac{\partial\xi_{2}}{\partial\nu_{S}^{\prime}}-\frac{\partial\xi_{2}}{\partial\tau_{S}^{\prime}}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{S}^{\prime},\\ \frac{\partial\xi_{2}}{\partial\nu_{N}^{\prime}}+\frac{\partial\xi_{2}}{\partial\tau_{N}^{\prime}}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{N}^{\prime}.\\ \end{cases}

The existence of a (possibly non-unique) solution ξ2∈H1​(Ω′)\xi_{2}\in H^{1}(\Omega^{\prime}) of (4.35)-(4.38) follows from Lemma 4.4.4.2 of [Gri85] with Ω=Ω′,𝒟=ΓW′,𝒩=ΓE′∪ΓS′∪ΓN′,f=−ψ1​y′−ψ2​x′\Omega=\Omega^{\prime},\mathscr{D}=\Gamma_{W}^{\prime},\mathscr{N}=\Gamma_{E}^{\prime}\cup\Gamma_{S}^{\prime}\cup\Gamma_{N}^{\prime},f=-\psi_{1y^{\prime}}-\psi_{2x^{\prime}}. Integrating (4.35)2\eqref{eq:eq6.31}_{2} with respect to y′y^{\prime} and using the boundary condition ( ♯ ‣ 4.1.2)3, we obtain a solution ξ1\xi_{1} which belongs to H1​(Ω′)H^{1}(\Omega^{\prime}).

In conclusion, in the new coordinate system (x′,y′)(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}), we find a (possibly non-unique) solution Ξ\Xi that belongs to V¯♯\overline{V}^{\sharp}, and solves the problem 𝒫​Ξ=Ψ\mathcal{P}\Xi=\Psi. Transforming back to the original system (x,y)(x,y) and the original variables Θ\Theta, we obtain Θ¯∈V¯\overline{\Theta}\in\overline{V} satisfying 𝒯∗​Θ¯=Ψ\mathcal{T}^{*}\overline{\Theta}=\Psi.

The proof of the uniqueness in 𝒟⁡(𝒯∗)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{T}^{*}) is the same as in the proof of Proposition 4.1. Therefore, the proof of Proposition 4.2 is complete. ∎

4.2. The mixed subcritical case

We are now ready to study the stationary 2D shallow water equations operator for the elliptic-hyperbolic case when Δ=u02+v02−g​ϕ0<0\Delta=u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0}<0, that is

(4.39) u02+v02<g​ϕ0,implying​u02<g​ϕ0,v02<g​ϕ0.u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 5.0pt\text{implying}\hskip 5.0ptu_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 3.0ptv_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0}.

In order to specify the boundary conditions, we recall the decoupled system (1.13). For ζ\zeta, we need to assign the boundary conditions at x=0x=0 and y=0y=0 since u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are both positive. For ξ\xi and η\eta, as we see in Remark 4.1 and Theorem 4.2, by taking into account the energy estimates, we can assign different kinds of boundary conditions for ξ\xi and η\eta which are suitable for the well-posedness. Here, we assign the boundary conditions for ξ\xi at x=0x=0 and y=0y=0, and the boundary conditions for η\eta at x=L1x=L_{1} and y=L2y=L_{2}. In conclusion, the boundary conditions for UU are

(4.40) {ξ=v0u−u0v=0,ζ=u0u+v0v+gϕ=0, on ΓW∪ΓS={x=0}∪{y=0},η≃ϕ=0, on ΓE∪ΓN={x=L1}∪{y=L2}.\begin{cases}\xi=v_{0}u-u_{0}v=0,\;\zeta=u_{0}u+v_{0}v+g\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}\cup\Gamma_{S}=\{x=0\}\cup\{y=0\},\\ \eta\simeq\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{E}\cup\Gamma_{N}=\{x=L_{1}\}\cup\{y=L_{2}\}.\end{cases}

We then define the function space

𝒟(A)={U∈H=L2(Ω)3,𝒜U∈H, and U satisfies (4.40)},\mathcal{D}(A)=\{U\in H=L^{2}(\Omega)^{3},\quad\mathcal{A}U\in H,\text{ and }U\text{ satisfies }\eqref{eq:eq7.1}\},\\

and set A​U=𝒜​U,∀U∈𝒟⁡(A)AU=\mathcal{A}U,\,\forall U\in\mathcal{D}(A).

4.2.1. Positivity of AA and its adjoint A∗A^{*}

We use the notations ξ,η,ζ\xi,\eta,\zeta and PP defined in (1.11) and set Ξ=(ξ,η,ζ)t\Xi=(\xi,\eta,\zeta)^{t}, so that U=P​ΞU=P\Xi. With the diagonalization (1.12), we compute for U∈𝒟⁡(A)U\in\mathcal{D}(A):

(4.41) ⟨A​U,U⟩H=∫Ω(u0​ux+v0​uy+g​ϕx)​u+(u0​vx+v0​vy+g​ϕy)​v+gϕ0​(u0​ϕx+v0​ϕy+ϕ0​(ux+vy))​ϕ​d​x​d​y=⟨S0​ℰ1​Ux+S0​ℰ2​Uy,U⟩H=⟨Pt​S0​ℰ1​P​Ξx+Pt​S0​ℰ2​P​Ξy,Ξ⟩H=∫Ω(ξ,η)​1u02+v02​((u0g​v0κ1g​v0κ1−u0)​(ξη)x+(v0−g​u0κ1−g​u0κ1−v0)​(ξη)y)​d​x​d​y+1u02+v02∫Ωζ(u0ζx+v0ζy)dxdy.\begin{split}\langle AU,U\rangle_{H}&=\int_{\Omega}(u_{0}u_{x}+v_{0}u_{y}+g\phi_{x})u+(u_{0}v_{x}+v_{0}v_{y}+g\phi_{y})v\\ &\hskip 20.0pt+\frac{g}{\phi_{0}}(u_{0}\phi_{x}+v_{0}\phi_{y}+\phi_{0}(u_{x}+v_{y}))\phi\text{d}x\text{d}y\\ &=\langle S_{0}\mathcal{E}_{1}U_{x}+S_{0}\mathcal{E}_{2}U_{y},U\rangle_{H}\\ &=\langle P^{t}S_{0}\mathcal{E}_{1}P\Xi_{x}+P^{t}S_{0}\mathcal{E}_{2}P\Xi_{y},\Xi\rangle_{H}\\ &=\int_{\Omega}(\xi,\eta)\frac{1}{u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}}\bigg(\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}&\frac{gv_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}\\ \frac{gv_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}&-u_{0}\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\xi\\ \eta\end{pmatrix}_{x}+\begin{pmatrix}v_{0}&-\frac{gu_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}\\ -\frac{gu_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}&-v_{0}\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\xi\\ \eta\end{pmatrix}_{y}\bigg)\text{d}x\text{d}y\\ &\hskip 20.0pt+\frac{1}{u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}}\int_{\Omega}\zeta(u_{0}\zeta_{x}+v_{0}\zeta_{y})\text{d}x\text{d}y.\\ \end{split}

We now need to show that J0,J1J_{0},J_{1} in the right-hand side of (4.41) are both non-negative. According to Theorem 4.2 with

(4.42) 𝒯​(ξη)=1u02+v02​(u0g​v0κ1g​v0κ1−u0)​(ξη)x+1u02+v02​(v0−g​u0κ1−g​u0κ1−v0)​(ξη)y,\mathcal{T}\begin{pmatrix}\xi\\ \eta\end{pmatrix}=\frac{1}{u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}}\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}&\frac{gv_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}\\ \frac{gv_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}&-u_{0}\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\xi\\ \eta\end{pmatrix}_{x}+\frac{1}{u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}}\begin{pmatrix}v_{0}&-\frac{gu_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}\\ -\frac{gu_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}&-v_{0}\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\xi\\ \eta\end{pmatrix}_{y},

we find that J0≥0J_{0}\geq 0. For J1J_{1}, by density Theorem 2.1 applied with θ=ζ,λ=u0/v0,Γ=ΓW∪ΓS\theta=\zeta,\lambda=u_{0}/v_{0},\Gamma=\Gamma_{W}\cup\Gamma_{S}, we see that the integration by parts is valid for J1J_{1}, and we find

J1=12​(u02+v02)​(∫0L2u0​ζ2|x=0x=L1​d​y+∫0L1v0​ζ2|y=0y=L2​d​x)≥0,J_{1}=\frac{1}{2(u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2})}\Big(\int_{0}^{L_{2}}u_{0}\zeta^{2}\Big|_{x=0}^{x=L_{1}}\text{d}y+\int_{0}^{L_{1}}v_{0}\zeta^{2}\Big|_{y=0}^{y=L_{2}}\text{d}x\Big)\geq 0,

where the last inequality follows from the boundary conditions for ζ=u0​u+v0​v+g​ϕ\zeta=u_{0}u+v_{0}v+g\phi and the assumption u0,v0>0u_{0},v_{0}>0.

Combining the results for J0J_{0} and J1J_{1}, we obtain that ⟨A​U,U⟩H≥0\langle AU,U\rangle_{H}\geq 0. Note that here, because the part of the operator AA which is elliptic gives some additional regularity, we did not need to use an approximation argument to show that ⟨A​U,U⟩H≥0,∀U∈𝒟⁡(A)\langle AU,U\rangle_{H}\geq 0,\,\forall U\in\mathcal{D}(A), unlike in the previous cases.

We now turn to the adjoint A∗A^{*}. In the mixed subcritical case, the formal definition of A∗A^{*} can also be treated similarly as in Subsection 3.1.1, we thus omit the details. The adjoint differential operator 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*} is given by (3.7) again. In order to guarantee that U↦⟨A​U,U¯⟩HU\mapsto\langle AU,\overline{U}\rangle_{H} is continuous on 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A), the following boundary conditions in the (ξ,η,ζ)(\xi,\eta,\zeta) variables need to be satisfied (see (4.25) since the equations for ξ,η\xi,\eta are elliptic):

(4.43) {g​v0κ1ξ¯−u0η¯=0, on ΓW={x=0},ζ¯=u0ξ¯+g​v0κ1η¯=0, on ΓE={x=L1},−g​u0κ1ξ¯−v0η¯=0, on ΓS={y=0},ζ¯=v0ξ¯−g​u0κ1η¯=0, on ΓN={y=L2}.\begin{cases}\frac{gv_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}\bar{\xi}-u_{0}\bar{\eta}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}=\{x=0\},\\ \bar{\zeta}=u_{0}\bar{\xi}+\frac{gv_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}\bar{\eta}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{E}=\{x=L_{1}\},\\ -\frac{gu_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}\bar{\xi}-v_{0}\bar{\eta}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{S}=\{y=0\},\\ \bar{\zeta}=v_{0}\bar{\xi}-\frac{gu_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}\bar{\eta}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{N}=\{y=L_{2}\}.\end{cases}

Transforming back to the (u,v,ϕ)(u,v,\phi) variables, the boundary conditions read

(4.44) {gv02u¯−gv0u0v¯−u0κ12ϕ¯=0, on ΓW={x=0},u0v0u¯−u02v¯+gv0ϕ¯=u0u¯+v0v¯+gϕ¯=0, on ΓE={x=L1},gu0v0u¯−gu02v¯+v0κ12ϕ¯=0, on ΓS={y=0},v02u¯−v0u0v¯−gu0ϕ¯=u0u¯+v0v¯+gϕ¯=0, on ΓN={y=L2},\begin{cases}gv_{0}^{2}\bar{u}-gv_{0}u_{0}\bar{v}-u_{0}\kappa_{1}^{2}\bar{\phi}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}=\{x=0\},\\ u_{0}v_{0}\bar{u}-u_{0}^{2}\bar{v}+gv_{0}\bar{\phi}=u_{0}\bar{u}+v_{0}\bar{v}+g\bar{\phi}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{E}=\{x=L_{1}\},\\ gu_{0}v_{0}\bar{u}-gu_{0}^{2}\bar{v}+v_{0}\kappa_{1}^{2}\bar{\phi}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{S}=\{y=0\},\\ v_{0}^{2}\bar{u}-v_{0}u_{0}\bar{v}-gu_{0}\bar{\phi}=u_{0}\bar{u}+v_{0}\bar{v}+g\bar{\phi}=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{N}=\{y=L_{2}\},\end{cases}

which are more complicated than the boundary conditions (4.40), since some elliptic modes are hidden in the operator AA. We conclude that (see also (4.29))

𝒟(A∗)={U¯∈H=L2(Ω)3,A∗U¯∈H, and U¯ satisfies (4.44)},\mathcal{D}(A^{*})=\{\overline{U}\in H=L^{2}(\Omega)^{3},\quad A^{*}\overline{U}\in H,\text{ and }\overline{U}\text{ satisfies \eqref{eq:eq7.4}}\},

and set A∗​U¯=𝒜∗​U¯,∀U¯∈𝒟⁡(A∗)A^{*}\overline{U}=\mathcal{A}^{*}\overline{U},\,\forall\overline{U}\in\mathcal{D}(A^{*}).

The proof of the positivity of A∗A^{*} is similar to that of AA where we need to use Theorem 4.4 for the elliptic mode hidden in the operator A∗A^{*}, we thus omit it here.

5. Existence and uniqueness results and additional remarks

In this section we aim to combine the results of the previous sections and to investigate the well-posedness for Eqs. (1.1) associated with the suitable initial and boundary conditions that we have introduced. Here again, we consider the case of homogeneous boundary conditions, and give below a remark about the non-homogeneous boundary conditions.

As we have already seen in the previous sections, we have two cases to consider depending on the sign of Δ=u02+v02−g​ϕ0\Delta=u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0}, and there are four sub-cases for the case when Δ=u02+v02−g​ϕ0\Delta=u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0} is positive. In the following, we list these cases and their corresponding boundary conditions.

We first consider the fully hyperbolic case, hence we assume that

Δ=u02+v02−g​ϕ0>0,\Delta=u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0}>0,

and as we have already seen, this leads to four sub-cases:

The supercritical case. The assumption is

(5.1) u02>g​ϕ0,v02>g​ϕ0,u_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0},\hskip 6.0ptv_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0},

and the corresponding boundary conditions are

(5.1′) {u=v=ϕ=0, on ΓW={x=0},u=v=ϕ=0, on ΓS={y=0};\begin{cases}u=v=\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}=\{x=0\},\\ u=v=\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{S}=\{y=0\};\end{cases}

The mixed hyperbolic case I. The assumption is

(5.2) u02​<g​ϕ0,v02>​g​ϕ0,u_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 6.0ptv_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0},

and the corresponding boundary conditions are

(5.2′) {v0u−u0v+κ0ϕ=u0u+v0v+gϕ=0, on ΓW={x=0},v0u−u0v−κ0ϕ=0, on ΓE={x=L1},u=v=ϕ=0, on ΓS={y=0};\begin{cases}v_{0}u-u_{0}v+\kappa_{0}\phi=u_{0}u+v_{0}v+g\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}=\{x=0\},\\ v_{0}u-u_{0}v-\kappa_{0}\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{E}=\{x=L_{1}\},\\ u=v=\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{S}=\{y=0\};\end{cases}

The mixed hyperbolic case II. The assumption is

(5.3) u02>g​ϕ0,v02<g​ϕ0,u_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0},\hskip 6.0ptv_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},

and the corresponding boundary conditions are

(5.3′) {v0u−u0v−κ0ϕ=u0u+v0v+gϕ=0, on ΓS={y=0},v0u−u0v+κ0ϕ=0, on ΓN={y=L2},u=v=ϕ=0, on ΓW={x=0};\begin{cases}v_{0}u-u_{0}v-\kappa_{0}\phi=u_{0}u+v_{0}v+g\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{S}=\{y=0\},\\ v_{0}u-u_{0}v+\kappa_{0}\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{N}=\{y=L_{2}\},\\ u=v=\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}=\{x=0\};\end{cases}

The fully hyperbolic subcritical case. The assumption is

(5.4) u02<g​ϕ0,v02<g​ϕ0,u02+v02>g​ϕ0,u_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 6.0ptv_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 6.0ptu_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}>g\phi_{0},

and the corresponding boundary conditions are

(5.4′) {v0u−u0v+κ0ϕ=u0u+v0v+gϕ=0, on ΓW={x=0},v0u−u0v−κ0ϕ=0, on ΓE={x=L1},v0u−u0v−κ0ϕ=u0u+v0v+gϕ=0, on ΓS={y=0},v0u−u0v+κ0ϕ=0, on ΓN={y=L2}.\begin{cases}v_{0}u-u_{0}v+\kappa_{0}\phi=u_{0}u+v_{0}v+g\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}=\{x=0\},\\ v_{0}u-u_{0}v-\kappa_{0}\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{E}=\{x=L_{1}\},\\ v_{0}u-u_{0}v-\kappa_{0}\phi=u_{0}u+v_{0}v+g\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{S}=\{y=0\},\\ v_{0}u-u_{0}v+\kappa_{0}\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{N}=\{y=L_{2}\}.\end{cases}

We then consider the elliptic-hyperbolic case where

Δ=u02+v02−g​ϕ0<0,\Delta=u_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}-g\phi_{0}<0,

and this leads to only one case, which we also call the mixed subcritical case.

The mixed subcritical case. The assumption is

(5.5) u02<g​ϕ0,v02<g​ϕ0,u02+v02<g​ϕ0,u_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 6.0ptv_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},\hskip 6.0ptu_{0}^{2}+v_{0}^{2}<g\phi_{0},

and the corresponding boundary conditions are

(5.5′) {v0u−u0v=u0u+v0v+gϕ=0, on ΓW∪ΓS={x=0}∪{y=0},ϕ=0, on ΓE∪ΓN={x=L1}∪{y=L2}.\begin{cases}v_{0}u-u_{0}v=u_{0}u+v_{0}v+g\phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{W}\cup\Gamma_{S}=\{x=0\}\cup\{y=0\},\\ \phi=0,\text{ on }\Gamma_{E}\cup\Gamma_{N}=\{x=L_{1}\}\cup\{y=L_{2}\}.\end{cases}

If these constants u0,v0,ϕ0,gu_{0},v_{0},\phi_{0},g satisfy assumption (5.j)(5.j), we then define the domain of the unbounded operator AA:

𝒟(A)={U∈H=L2(Ω)3,AU∈H and U satisfies (5.j′)},\begin{split}\mathcal{D}(A)=\{U\in H=L^{2}(\Omega)^{3},\quad AU\in H\text{ and }U\text{ satisfies }(5.j^{\prime})\},\end{split}

where j∈{1,2,3,4,5}j\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}, indicating the five different cases.

We set B​U=(−f​v,f​u,0)tBU=(-fv,fu,0)^{t}, where ff is the Coriolis parameter; it is easy to see that BB is a linear continuous anti-self-adjoint (i.e. B∗=−BB^{*}=-B) operator on HH. We also set A0=A+BA_{0}=A+B, with 𝒟⁡(A0)=𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A_{0})=\mathcal{D}(A), and consider the adjoint A0∗=A∗+B∗A_{0}^{*}=A^{*}+B^{*}, with 𝒟⁡(A0∗)=𝒟⁡(A∗)\mathcal{D}(A_{0}^{*})=\mathcal{D}(A^{*}). Then we have

Theorem 5.1.

The operator −A0-A_{0} is the infinitesimal generator of a contraction semigroup on HH.

Proof.

According to [Yos80, HP74], it suffices to show that

  1. (i)

    A0A_{0} and A0∗A_{0}^{*} are both closed operators, and their domains 𝒟⁡(A0)\mathcal{D}(A_{0}) and 𝒟⁡(A0∗)\mathcal{D}(A_{0}^{*}) are dense in HH.

  2. (ii)

    A0A_{0} and A0∗A_{0}^{*} are both positive.

Noticing that BB is a linear continuous operator on HH and that ⟨B​U,U⟩=0\langle BU,U\rangle=0 and ⟨B∗​U,U⟩=0\langle B^{*}U,U\rangle=0 for all U∈HU\in H, we find that proving (i) and (ii) is equivalent to proving the following:

  1. (i′)

    AA and A∗A^{*} are both closed operators, and their domains 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) and 𝒟⁡(A∗)\mathcal{D}(A^{*}) are dense in HH.

  2. (ii′)

    AA and A∗A^{*} are both positive.

We already showed that AA and A∗A^{*} are both positive in the previous subsections, we thus only need to prove (i′). We establish the result for AA, and the proof for A∗A^{*} would be similar.

In all cases, observing that 𝒟​(Ω)3\mathcal{D}(\Omega)^{3} is included in 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) and dense in H=L2​(Ω)3H=L^{2}(\Omega)^{3}, we thus obtain that 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) is dense in HH. To show that AA is closed, consider a sequence {Un}n∈ℕ⊂𝒟⁡(A)\{U_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{D}(A) for which limn→∞Un=U\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}U_{n}=U in L2​(Ω)3L^{2}(\Omega)^{3} and limn→∞𝒜​Un=F\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{A}U_{n}=F in L2​(Ω)3L^{2}(\Omega)^{3}. By the L2L^{2}-convergence of {Un}n∈ℕ\{U_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, we first find that 𝒜​Un\mathcal{A}U_{n} converges to 𝒜​U\mathcal{A}U in the sense of distributions, which implies that 𝒜​U\mathcal{A}U equals FF in the sense of distributions. Since FF belongs to L2​(Ω)3L^{2}(\Omega)^{3}, we obtain that 𝒜​U\mathcal{A}U belongs to L2​(Ω)3L^{2}(\Omega)^{3}, too. Thus, we have U,𝒜​U∈L2​(Ω)3U,\mathcal{A}U\in L^{2}(\Omega)^{3}, which shows that the traces of UU are well-defined thanks to Proposition 2.1. By Proposition 2.1 again, the traces of UnU_{n} converge weakly to the traces of UU in the appropriate space H−1H^{-1}, so that UU satisfies the boundary conditions (5.j′)(5.j^{\prime}), where j∈{1,2,3,4,5}j\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}. Therefore, we conclude that U∈𝒟⁡(A)U\in\mathcal{D}(A). Hence AA is closed, and the proof is complete. ∎

We now consider the whole system of 2D linearized Shallow Water Equations, namely (1.1) and introduce the initial and boundary conditions. As we discussed before, the boundary conditions are (5.j′),j∈{1,2,3,4,5}(5.j^{\prime}),j\in\{1,2,3,4,5\} depending on the case we are considering, and all these boundary conditions are taken into account in the domain 𝒟⁡(A0)\mathcal{D}(A_{0}) of A0A_{0}. Finally if we add the initial conditions:

(5.6) U⁡(0)=(u⁡(0),v⁡(0),ϕ⁡(0))=U0=(u0,v0,ϕ0),U(0)=(u(0),v(0),\phi(0))=U^{0}=(u^{0},v^{0},\phi^{0}),

then the initial and boundary value problem consisting of Eqs. (1.1), (5.j′),j∈{1,2,3,4,5}(5.j^{\prime}),j\in\{1,2,3,4,5\} and (5.6) is equivalent to the abstract initial value problem

(5.7) {d​Ud​t+A0​U=F,U⁡(0)=U0.\begin{cases}\frac{\text{d}U}{\text{d}t}+A_{0}U=F,\\ U(0)=U^{0}.\end{cases}

Note that F=(Fu,Fv,Fϕ)F=(F_{u},F_{v},F_{\phi}) which does not appear in (1.1) is added here for mathematical generality and to study the case of non-homogeneous boundary conditions. Thanks to Theorem 5.1 this problem is now solved by the Hille-Yoshida theorem and we have:

Theorem 5.2.

Let H,A0H,A_{0} and 𝒟⁡(A0)\mathcal{D}(A_{0}) be defined as before. Then the initial value problem (5.7) is well-posed. That is,

  1. i)

    for every U0∈HU^{0}\in H, and F∈L1​(0,T,H)F\in L^{1}(0,T;H), the problem (5.7) admits a unique weak solution U∈𝒞⁡([0,T],H)U\in\mathcal{C}([0,T];H) satisfying

    U⁡(t)=S⁡(t)​U0+∫0tS⁡(t−s)​F​(s)​d​s,∀t∈[0,T],U(t)=S(t)U^{0}+\int_{0}^{t}S(t-s)F(s)\text{\emph{d}}s,\,\forall t\in[0,T],

    where (S⁡(t))t≥0(S(t))_{t\geq 0} is the contraction semigroup generated by the operator −A0-A_{0};

  2. ii)

    for every U0∈𝒟⁡(A0)U^{0}\in\mathcal{D}(A_{0}), and F∈L1​(0,T,H)F\in L^{1}(0,T;H), with F′=d​F/d​t∈L1​(0,T,H)F^{\prime}=\text{\emph{d}}F/\text{\emph{d}}t\in L^{1}(0,T;H), the problem (5.7) has a unique strong solution UU such that

    U∈𝒞⁡([0,T],𝒟⁡(A0)),d​Ud​t∈𝒞⁡([0,T],H).U\in\mathcal{C}\big([0,T];\mathcal{D}(A_{0})\big),\hskip 6.0pt\frac{\text{\emph{d}}U}{\text{\emph{d}}t}\in\mathcal{C}\big([0,T];H\big).

We conclude with three remarks concerning the extension of this work to other domains, the connections with the Primitive Equations of the atmosphere and the oceans and with the issue of non-homogeneous boundary conditions.

Remark 5.1.

It is likely that much of the results concerning the fully hyperbolic case can be extended to more general convex polygonal domains instead of a rectangle, or probably more general polygonal-like domains. However, in the part concerning the elliptic-hyperbolic case, we use some of Grisvard’s results which require very restrictive conditions on the angles. Also we preferred to consider a rectangle domain to stay close from the initial motivation of this study in LAMs.

Remark 5.2.

The linearized 3D inviscid Primitive Equations of the atmosphere and the oceans can be written:

(5.8) {ut+U0​ux+V0​uy−f​v+ϕx=0,vt+U0​vx+V0​vy+f​u+ϕy=0,Tt+U0​Tx+V0​Ty+N2​T0g​w=0,ux+vy+wz=0,ϕz=g​TT0,\begin{cases}u_{t}+U_{0}u_{x}+V_{0}u_{y}-fv+\phi_{x}=0,\\ v_{t}+U_{0}v_{x}+V_{0}v_{y}+fu+\phi_{y}=0,\\ T_{t}+U_{0}T_{x}+V_{0}T_{y}+N^{2}\frac{T_{0}}{g}w=0,\\ u_{x}+v_{y}+w_{z}=0,\\ \phi_{z}=\frac{gT}{T_{0}},\end{cases}

where (u,v,w)(u,v,w) is the velocity of the water, (u,v)(u,v) the horizontal velocity, TT the temperature, ϕ\phi a multiple of the pressure, gg the gravitational acceleration, and N2N^{2} denotes the Brunt-Va¨\ddot{\text{a}}isa¨\ddot{\text{a}}la¨\ddot{\text{a}} (buoyancy) frequency satisfying

N2=−gρ0​d​ρd​z,N^{2}=-\frac{g}{\rho_{0}}\frac{d\rho}{dz},

and U0>0,V0>0,ρ0>0U_{0}>0,V_{0}>0,\rho_{0}>0 and T0>0T_{0}>0 are reference average values of the density and the temperature.

We refer to [RTT08b] for a systematic discussion in the case when V0=0V_{0}=0. Using the normal modes expansion for (5.8) (see details in [RTT08b]), we obtain the equations for the non-zero modes (un,vn,ϕn,λn)(u_{n},v_{n},\phi_{n},\lambda_{n}) which read (the indices nn are dropped for the sake of simplicity):

(5.9) {ut+U0​ux+V0​uy−f​v−1λ​ψx=0,vt+U0​vx+V0​vy+f​u−1λ​ψy=0,ψt+U0​ψx+V0​ψy−N2λ​(ux+vy)=0,\begin{cases}u_{t}+U_{0}u_{x}+V_{0}u_{y}-fv-\frac{1}{\lambda}\psi_{x}=0,\\ v_{t}+U_{0}v_{x}+V_{0}v_{y}+fu-\frac{1}{\lambda}\psi_{y}=0,\\ \psi_{t}+U_{0}\psi_{x}+V_{0}\psi_{y}-\frac{N^{2}}{\lambda}(u_{x}+v_{y})=0,\end{cases}

where ψ=−λ​ϕ\psi=-\lambda\phi and λ\lambda is positive. Observing that (5.9) has the same form as the shallow water equation (1.1) if we replace ϕ\phi and gg in (1.1) by −ψ-\psi and λ−1\lambda^{-1}, we thus can obtain a well-posedness result (see Theorem 5.2) for (5.9). The equations for the zero mode are

(5.10) {ut+U0​ux+V0​uy−f​v+1λ​ϕx=0,vt+U0​vx+V0​vy+f​u+1λ​ϕy=0,ux+vy=0.\begin{cases}u_{t}+U_{0}u_{x}+V_{0}u_{y}-fv+\frac{1}{\lambda}\phi_{x}=0,\\ v_{t}+U_{0}v_{x}+V_{0}v_{y}+fu+\frac{1}{\lambda}\phi_{y}=0,\\ u_{x}+v_{y}=0.\end{cases}

Following the same argument as for the zero mode in [RTT08b] and [CST10], we can also obtain the well-posedness result for (5.10). Therefore, we can obtain a well-posedness result for the whole system (5.8) with suitable boundary conditions and initial conditions as in Section 4 of [RTT08b]. The details will appear elsewhere.

Remark 5.3.

In this remark, we briefly show how our results can be extended to the case of non-homogeneous boundary conditions, that is we want to solve (1.1) with (5.j′)(5.j^{\prime}) (j∈{1,2,3,4,5}j\in\left\{1,2,3,4,5\right\}) in which the boundary conditions are now non-homogeneous, and with initial condition (5.6). We write the problem as follows

(5.11) {Ut+𝒜​U+B​U=F,U⁡(0)=U0,+suitable non-homogeneous boundary conditions.\begin{cases}U_{t}+\mathcal{A}U+BU=F,\\ U(0)=U^{0},\\ +\text{suitable non-homogeneous boundary conditions}.\end{cases}

We assume that the boundary data are inferred from a function UgU^{g} which is defined on Ω×[0,T]\Omega\times[0,T], and we remark that this assumption is reasonable since we have a lifting result for the domain Ω\Omega (see Lemma 1.5.2.3 in [Gri85]). We now set

U=U′+Ug.U=U^{\prime}+U^{g}.

Then U′U^{\prime} will be sought as the solution of the problem:

(5.12) {Ut′+𝒜​U′+B​U′=F′,U′​(0)=U0−Ug|t=0,+suitable homogeneous boundary conditions,\begin{cases}U^{\prime}_{t}+\mathcal{A}U^{\prime}+BU^{\prime}=F^{\prime},\\ U^{\prime}(0)=U^{0}-U^{g}|_{t=0},\\ +\text{suitable homogeneous boundary conditions},\end{cases}

where

F′=F−Utg−𝒜​Ug−B​Ug.F^{\prime}=F-U^{g}_{t}-\mathcal{A}U^{g}-BU^{g}.

Observing that U′∈𝒟⁡(A)U^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(A) if U′U^{\prime} is smooth enough (suitable homogeneous boundary conditions), we then rewrite (5.12) as the linear evolution equation

(5.13) {d​U′d​t+A0​U′=F′,U′​(0)=U0−Ug|t=0,\begin{cases}\frac{\text{\emph{d}}U^{\prime}}{\text{\emph{d}}t}+A_{0}U^{\prime}=F^{\prime},\\ U^{\prime}(0)=U^{0}-U^{g}|_{t=0},\end{cases}

where A0=A+BA_{0}=A+B with 𝒟⁡(A0)=𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A_{0})=\mathcal{D}(A). We already knew that A0A_{0} generates a contraction semigroup on HH (see Theorem 5.1). Therefore, if we assume that

(5.14) F,Ug,Utg,Uxg,Uyg∈L1​(0,T,H),U′​(0)∈H,F,\,U^{g},\,U^{g}_{t},\,U^{g}_{x},\,U^{g}_{y}\in L^{1}(0,T;H),\quad U^{\prime}(0)\in H,

then the problem (5.13) admits a unique weak solution U′∈𝒞⁡([0,T],H)U^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}([0,T];H) by the Hille-Yoshida theorem. We could also obtain a strong solution U′U^{\prime} of (5.13) if we assume more regularity on the data F,Ug,U0F,\,U^{g},\,U^{0}, and we omit the details here. Typically we would supplement (5.14) with

(5.15) Ft,Utg,Ut​tg,Ux​tg,Uy​tg∈L1​(0,T,H),F_{t},\,U_{t}^{g},\,U^{g}_{tt},\,U^{g}_{xt},\,U^{g}_{yt}\in L^{1}(0,T;H),

and

(5.16) U′​(0)∈𝒟⁡(A0).U^{\prime}(0)\in\mathcal{D}(A_{0}).

Note that the later condition contains the usual compatibility conditions at t=0t=0 between U0|∂ΩU^{0}|_{\partial\Omega} and Ug​(t=0)|∂ΩU^{g}(t=0)|_{\partial\Omega} (see [RM74]).
